塤,Xun (instrument),吹奏與氣息樂器,亞洲／東亞（中國）,樂器教: Xun,Xun (instrument),Aerophones,Asia / East Asia (China),instrument teaching,world instruments,instrument introduction
The xun is an egg-shaped vessel flute from China, an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.221.42. It has a blow hole at the top, at least three fingerholes in front and two thumb holes behind, and modern instruments may have eight to eleven holes; it looks like an ocarina but has no fipple, so the player has to adjust the angle of the breath and can turn the body to fine-tune the pitch. From the Qin and Han dynasties onward it was used mostly in court ritual music, sacrifices and ceremonies, and in the traditional Chinese orchestra it takes the alto part, with a deep, mournful, full timbre.
塤為氣鳴器皿笛，發聲體即卵形或橢圓形腔體，最初以石、燒製黏土或骨製成，後來以陶土: The xun is a vessel aerophone whose sounding element is the egg-shaped or oval cavity; it was first made of stone, fired clay or bone, and later mainly of pottery clay or ceramic, occasionally bamboo. Traditional making takes clean clay, kneads it with water, shapes the blank, forms the holes, polishes it and fires it in a kiln; in the Shang dynasty pottery, stone and bone forms are found. The source does not state the material of the blow-hole edge, the lining of the fingerholes or any other fitting.
塤的音色溫潤而蒼涼，具有深沉的暗沉質感，帶著古老而神秘的氣息。其音域相對較窄，主: The xun's timbre is warm and desolate, with a deep, dark quality and an ancient, mysterious air. Its range is fairly narrow, mostly in the middle and low register, and the tone is husky and throaty, like an old singer humming quietly. Its resonance is distinctive: it relies on the air vibrating inside the spherical cavity, which gives the sound rich overtones. Compared with the clear brightness of the flute, the xun's timbre is more inward and restrained; compared with the ocarina it is more vigorous and forceful. Its sound suits distant, quiet, sorrowful moods and is often used to create an archaic, meditative atmosphere; it has strong historical reach and emotional power.
塤起源於中國，距今約七千年，與石器時代狩獵活動有關。早期陶塤出土於河姆渡與仰韶遺: The xun originated in China about seven thousand years ago and is connected with Stone Age hunting. Early pottery xun have been excavated at Hemudu and Yangshao; they are mostly oval or olive-shaped and have only a blow hole and no fingerholes. By the Xia dynasty the xun had three fingerholes and could play a four-note series; in the Shang dynasty the form settled down, mostly egg-shaped with a flat base, pottery, stone and bone versions appeared, and the holes increased to five, enough for whole tones and semitones within a single octave. In the Zhou dynasty it became a common court instrument, its design varying with banquet music or ceremony; after the Qin and Han it was used mainly in ritual music, sacrifices and ceremonies. It faded from use from the Qing dynasty onward and was taken up again in the 1970s and 80s after excavations such as the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng; modern versions add fingerholes to extend the range.
將吹口對準嘴唇，穩定吹氣入管。將吹口對準嘴唇，以穩定的氣流吹入管身。嘴唇的形狀和: Set the mouthpiece against the lips and blow steadily into the pipe. Set the mouthpiece against the lips and blow a steady airstream into the body. The shape and tension of the lips affect pitch and timbre. The fingers press the fingerholes or keys to change the sounding length and so control pitch.
